17.0.0.en: "According to their journeys": the children of Israel traveled as groups, each group pitching its tents beside the other, and when they moved from place to place they moved one group after another, and also according to the places through which they passed and from which God commanded them to move on to another.

17.0.1.en: Rephidim: its meaning is resting places, and it is in the middle of the wilderness of Sinai toward the south.

17.0.2.en: The children of Israel moved from the wilderness of Sin southward to a place called Rephidim, and it was barren, with no water in it.

17.1.0.en: The people murmured against Moses because of their thirst and demanded that he and Aaron bring water, and he rebuked them for their murmuring against God after they had seen great wonders such as the ten plagues, the crossing of the Red Sea, the turning of the bitter water into sweet water at Marah, and the sending of the manna and the quails...

17.2.0.en: The people fell not only into murmuring but also into despair because of the severity of the thirst, but sadly they did not lift up their prayers to God, as they felt that they would die of thirst.

17.3.0.en: Because of the people's great agitation and murmuring, Moses was afraid and cried out to God to save him from their hands, because they were almost ready to stone him. This shows Moses' faith in his taking refuge in God, but there is in him some weakness of faith because of his fear of the people.

17.3.1.en: Take refuge in God in all your afflictions, however harsh, and even if all people rise up against you, trust that He is able to save you and to work miracles for you.

17.4.0.en: God answered Moses and promised to solve the problem by his going on before the people with his rod, so that they might be reassured that God was with him, because God had worked many miracles with this rod, and He commanded him to take with him some of the elders of the children of Israel to be witnesses of the miracle that would happen, which was the coming out of water from the solid rock.

17.5.0.en: The rock: it was a rock known to Moses, which was either beside the bush or beside which the pillar of fire used to stand.

17.5.1.en: Horeb: the name of the region in which Mount Sinai lies.

17.5.2.en: God commanded Moses to strike the rock so that water would come out, and he did so, and the water came out before the elders of Israel. The rock signifies Christ, who quenches our thirst with the waters of His Holy Spirit. The rod signifies the Cross that Christ bore for us: the rod struck the rock, and likewise through His crucifixion we received the Holy Spirit. The rod also signifies the Law, which Christ fulfilled and then died and redeemed us, and it also signifies the spear with which Christ was pierced on the Cross, and blood and water came out of His side.

17.6.2.en: Another place at Kadesh was also called by this name (Num 20:13) because of the likeness of what happened there to this incident.

17.6.3.en: Moses called the place where the water came out of the rock Massah and Meribah, to remind the people that they had fallen into temptation and murmured and quarreled with God, but God in His tenderness gave them water.

17.6.4.en: Remember your sins at all times so that you may always repent, and so thank God and receive His mercies.

17.7.0.en: Amalek: they are the descendants of Eliphaz the son of Esau, and there was enmity between them and the descendants of Jacob, perhaps because of Jacob's taking the birthright from their forefather Esau. They lived in the south of Palestine and Syria, and they were enraged when they saw God's blessing in the number of the children of Israel, so they attacked them.

17.7.1.en: Joshua: he is the son of Nun of the tribe of Ephraim, and the meaning of his name is God saves; he was one of the spies whom Moses sent to spy out the Promised Land (Num 13, 14) and became Moses' successor in leading the people and bringing them into the Promised Land (Num 13:8). An army of tall men attacked them in the wilderness of Sinai for the first time, and they called them Amalekites. So Moses sent Joshua to lead the army and fight Amalek, while he went up on a hill to pray for them and held in his hand the rod of God, to strengthen the people's faith in God, who had worked many miracles for him with this rod, and so that he might ask Him to intervene for victory over Amalek.

17.7.2.en: Joining your spiritual striving with your prayer guarantees you victory, so do not fear your enemies, however mighty, as long as you are faithful in your works and pray.

17.8.0.en: Hur: one of Moses' close disciples, of the tribe of Judah, and the grandfather of Bezaleel, who led the craftsmen who made the tabernacle of the congregation (Ex 31:1); some think that he was the husband of Miriam, the sister of Moses.

17.8.1.en: Joshua obeyed Moses and led the people to fight Amalek, while Moses went up the hill with his brother Aaron and one of Moses' pious disciples, Hur, to help him in prayer.

17.8.2.en: Important spiritual meanings appear from this, which are:

17.8.3.en: 1- The importance of prayer accompanying spiritual striving.

17.8.4.en: 2- The people's sharing with the leader or servant in prayer and every spiritual work, for this cooperation encourages souls and God rejoices in this unity.

17.8.5.en: 3- Despite the strength of the leader or servant, he needs the help of other servants, namely Aaron and Hur, in addition to Joshua and all who fight with him.

17.8.6.en: How sweet it is for brethren to gather together for prayer, for God rejoices in the prayer of the congregation more than in the prayer of the individual; so would that you would take care to have common prayer in your home, if not every day then at least every week.

17.9.0.en: In prayer Moses lifted up his hands, so that he was in the form of a cross, and by the Cross and prayer Israel prevailed over Amalek. When he grew tired and his hands dropped a little, Amalek prevailed over Israel; so he strengthened himself and lifted up his hands again, and Israel regained its victory over the enemies, and then if he grew tired and his hands dropped, Amalek would return and prevail. God permitted this to declare the importance of joining prayer with the Cross, in whose form Moses was when he lifted up his hands to pray.

17.9.1.en: From this it appears that Moses here was a type of Christ in the following:

17.9.2.en: 1- Moses lifted up his hands for prayer like Christ, who lifted up His hands on the Cross.

17.9.3.en: 2- Moses' bodily weakness appeared and he needed Aaron and Hur to hold up his hands, and Christ in the garden of Gethsemane, when He was crushed with pain as a man, was visited by an angel to strengthen Him.

17.9.4.en: 3- The rod in Moses' hand was a banner for the people to confirm their faith, and the Cross is the sign of victory for Christians.

17.9.5.en: 4- Moses kept his hands stretched out until the going down of the sun, like Christ, who remained crucified until He died at the ninth hour, and they took His body down at sunset.

17.9.6.en: 5- Moses was between Aaron and Hur, and Christ was crucified between two thieves.

17.9.7.en: 6- Moses by his prayer was an intercessor for his people before God, and Christ is the only atoning Intercessor for the sins of His people.

17.10.0.en: When Moses grew tired from much prayer, they seated him on a stone, and Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on each side. This confirms the importance of perseverance in prayer and also the importance of the work of every individual in the Church, for without Hur and Aaron the victory would not have been accomplished, and not only without Moses.

17.11.0.en: In the end Israel's victory over Amalek was accomplished, so the enemies were afraid, and Israel continued on its way in the wilderness of Sinai.

17.12.0.en: God asked Moses to write down this victory in a book so that Israel would always remember God's supporting power. And He stressed to Joshua the importance of this victory, because God knows that Joshua will be the leader after Moses, so that He might encourage the people not to fear the strong inhabitants of the land of Canaan when they enter it. Amalek signifies Satan, so God promised his defeat and destruction, so that His people would not fear the enemy demons, however strong, and to declare the punishment of the wicked who persist in their evil, who must perish like Amalek.

17.12.1.en: Remember God's promises, and do not be disturbed by the threats of the enemies and their strength.

17.13.0.en: Moses expressed his thanks to God by building an altar and offering sacrifices to God upon it, and he called it "Jehovahnissi," that is, God is my banner and my standard, because he had triumphed and the name of God was exalted over Amalek and over all the enemies.

17.14.1.en: "The throne of the Lord": the people of Israel.

17.14.2.en: Because Amalek attacked the people of God, he attacked God Himself, therefore God rose up against him in a war that lasted many years until Amalek perished in the days of David. Who can stand before God?!

17.14.3.en: Do not disobey God or defy Him with your sins lest He be angry with you, and do not persist in them lest they destroy you, and if you sin, hasten to repentance.

17.14.4.en: Jethro's visit and advice to Moses

18.0.0.en: Zipporah and her two sons went out with Moses to the land of Egypt, and she lived through the events of the ten plagues and then crossed the Red Sea with him. In the wilderness of Sinai it seems that she hastened to her father to bring him the good news of God's work with the children of Israel.

18.1.0.en: Jethro took his daughter Zipporah and his grandsons Gershom and Eliezer and set out to visit Moses and congratulate him on God's work with him.

18.1.1.en: Gershom: its meaning is stranger, because Moses was a stranger and sojourner in Egypt.

18.1.2.en: Eliezer: its meaning is God helps and has mercy, because God delivered Moses from the hand of Pharaoh on account of his killing the Egyptian man (ch. 2). Moses may have named his sons these names by the spirit of prophecy, because he knew the work of God that would happen with him.

18.2.0.en: Jethro sent word by one of those working for Moses and told him of his arrival with Moses' wife and sons.

18.3.0.en: Moses went out with joy to receive his father-in-law, and so did his wife and sons, and his humility appears in that he bowed down to his father-in-law out of respect for him and esteem for his age, although he was a priest of idols. Perhaps this humility and love are what influenced Jethro, in addition to his hearing of God's work with him, so he glorified God and offered sacrifices to Him (v. 12).

18.3.1.en: Offer your love with humility to all, near and far, and you will win them and their hearts will open to the love of God.

18.4.0.en: Moses sat with his father-in-law and told him in detail of God's works with His people, which Jethro had heard about briefly before, and these matters include:

18.4.1.en: 1- How God delivered His people and brought them out of the land of Egypt by means of the ten plagues.

18.4.2.en: 2- After they went out of Egypt, when Pharaoh pursued them to bring them back, and how God rescued them from his hand by means of the pillar of cloud or fire and the parting of the Red Sea, and then Pharaoh and his army were drowned in the sea.

18.4.3.en: 3- How He rescued them from thirst on the way in the wilderness by turning the bitter water into sweet and bringing water out of the rock, and then rescued them from hunger by the manna and the quails.

18.5.0.en: God's works were great, so Jethro rejoiced in them and blessed God and glorified Him for rescuing His people from the hand of the mightiest of peoples at that time, the Egyptians.

18.6.0.en: In his glorifying God he exalted Him above all the pagan gods whom he worshipped, because His power, which appeared with Pharaoh and in the parting of the Red Sea, has no equal in the works of the pagan gods.

18.7.0.en: Continuing in glorifying God, Jethro offered sacrifices to Him. And when Aaron, Moses' brother, and the elders of Israel learned of the coming of Moses' father-in-law to visit him, they came to welcome him and ate with him, rejoicing in God's work and showing their love for Jethro and Moses.

18.7.1.en: Take care to thank God for all His works with you, and express your thanks by holy worship, works of goodness and service that you offer to others.

18.8.s.en: (3) The problem of crowding at the judging

18.8.0.en: Moses was accustomed to set aside days for judging the people in their problems, and the next day was set aside for that, so many people came, and Moses sat judging their problems from morning until evening, which was of course exhausting for him, in addition to the people's weariness from the long waiting.

18.9.0.en: Jethro was amazed at the crowding of all the people with all their problems upon one person, Moses, to judge between them.

18.10.0.en: Moses told Jethro that the people meet problems in their dealings and that he knows the law of God and so guides them and judges between them. From this appears:

18.10.1.en: 1- Moses' care, as a shepherd, for the problems of his people.

18.10.4.en: 4- He was a mediator between the people and God.

18.10.5.en: And God equipped him with wisdom and gave him bodily strength to bear these burdens despite his advanced age, for he was past eighty.

18.10.6.en: It is good to seek God's guidance in all the details of your life through prayer, the Holy Bible and the guidance of the father of confession, and trust that if you seek it He will guide you, and you will walk reassured, rejoicing in your walk with Him.

18.11.0.en: Jethro drew Moses' attention to the difficulty of the present situation, for two reasons:

18.11.1.en: 1- Moses' great exhaustion in judging all the people.

18.11.2.en: 2- The people's weariness from the long waiting.

18.12.0.en: He advised him to divide the work, so that Moses would devote himself to prayer and seeking God's counsel for the great cases, and would guide the people with the general rules and commandments so that they might please God.

18.13.0.en: He asked him to appoint assistants to lead the people, making some of them rulers of thousands, and each of them is helped by rulers of hundreds, and these are helped by rulers of fifties, and finally each of the rulers of fifties is helped by rulers of tens. In all the assistants the following is required:

18.13.1.en: 1- That they fear God and so hold to His commandments.

18.13.2.en: 2- Faithful and careful in their work.

18.13.3.en: 3- Not lovers of money and bribery, so that they are not influenced by the gifts of the wicked but please God and their conscience.

18.14.0.en: These assistants judge the small cases, while the great cases are referred to Moses himself.

18.15.0.en: "And God command thee so": God approves this counsel after you pray to Him.

18.15.1.en: In the end he told him that this counsel fulfills the carrying out of God's commandments and gives rest to him and to the people, so that they return to their dwellings at rest after their problems are solved.

18.15.2.en: Organizing every work and dividing it makes its execution easier, for wisdom is necessary in management, so take care to manage your life and organize everything.

18.16.0.en: Moses' humility appears in his obeying his father-in-law's counsel, for he is ready to learn from everyone, even the pagans, hearing the voice of God in every way that reaches him.

18.17.0.en: Moses chose assistants for himself and distributed the work among them, and reserved for himself only the great cases, as his father-in-law had advised him.

18.18.0.en: After Jethro had spent a period visiting Moses and was reassured about him, he returned to his country, Midian.

18.18.1.en: Be humble and learn from everyone, and you will hear the voice of God and advance in your life at all times. God speaks to you in many forms, and if you are humble you can hear.

18.18.2.en: Preparation for receiving the Ten Commandments
